craft_claim: Deadpan decays under repetition: each recurrence of the same flat-surface move reduces novelty and invites the reader to pre-cue the joke, after which the construction lands literally — so a piece should escalate rather than repeat, and re-arm the surprise sparingly.

supporting_evidence.location: book-level only (Appleton-Century-Crofts, 1971; xiv+336 pp.; page locator not verified)
supporting_evidence.note: Berlyne's collative-variable account (novelty, surprise, complexity drive arousal; repetition habituates) predicts decay of the deadpan surprise when the same cue recurs unchanged. Tier 2; page-level locator evidence-incomplete. The inverted-U arousal curve is unevenly replicated in later work.

Pre-cued audiences cannot be pretensed at: once the reader knows the voice is ironic, the pretense that produced the effect is transparent and inert. Tier 2; the stronger of the two supports for reader-cue budget.

Kharms keeps sentence mechanics constant while escalating stakes — variation lives in content, not in surface, which is the documented method for sustaining the tone without repetition collapse. Tier 3/4 practice anchor; translation-mediated.

counterevidence.note: The inverted-U relation between arousal and collative variables has had uneven empirical replication; the precise 'dose' cannot be fixed numerically. Bounds the claim: direction of decay is supported, exact thresholds are not.

scope: Sustained pieces (essay, story, chapter) using deadpan as the dominant tone. In single-sentence or headline uses saturation is not a concern. Thresholds in the card's dosage section are bounded writer-inference, not measured constants (evidence-incomplete: no deadpan-specific numeric study located).
exceptions: Deadpan held *unchanged* across an entire short work can succeed as a stylistic monoculture (the 'one register' essay) when the container promises it; the failure appears when the piece tries to *surprise* repeatedly from the same position.
